Trajan. A Roman emperor who ruled from AD 98 to 117. As the second of the Five Good Emperors, he was a highly successful soldier-emperor who presided over the greatest military expansion in Roman history, leading the empire to attain its maximum territorial extent by the time of his death.

He led successful campaigns to conquer Dacia, which is modern-day Romania, incorporating its vast gold mines into the empire. His victory in Dacia is famously commemorated by Trajan's Column, a massive triumphal column in Rome featuring a continuous spiralling bas-relief depicting the wars. He expanded the empire's eastern borders by annexing the Nabataean kingdom to form the province of Arabia Petraea, and later conquered parts of the Parthian Empire, including Armenia and Mesopotamia. The Roman Senate officially declared him optimus princeps, meaning "the best ruler." He implemented the Alimenta, an extensive welfare program that helped orphans and poor children throughout Italy.

His successor was Hadrian, a fellow Spaniard who consolidated Trajan's conquests and pulled back from some of his eastern expansions. His predecessor was Nerva, who adopted the popular general Trajan as his heir to avoid a civil war. Apollodorus of Damascus was his chief architect, who designed Trajan's Forum, Trajan's Column, and the massive bridge across the Danube.
